lessonRef.subject: mathematics
lessonRef.focus: deciding whether a model is consistent with data
lessonRef.title: Assessment preparation: deciding whether a model is consistent with data

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 88 and standard deviation 10. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 78 and 98?
choices: about 50%
about 68%
about 99.7%
about 95%

items.prompt: A researcher runs a randomised controlled experiment with participants randomly assigned to treatments. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.

items.prompt: A random sample of 625 people gives a sample proportion of 65%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±65%, giving 0% to 130%
±8%, giving 57% to 73%
±4%, giving 61% to 69%

items.prompt: In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 3 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 3% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 3% of simulations, which is not unusual.

items.prompt: A quantity is approximately normal with mean 146 and standard deviation 14. Approximately what percentage of values lie between 118 and 174?
choices: about 68%
about 50%
about 99.7%
about 95%

items.prompt: A researcher runs an observational study of volunteers who chose their own group. What kind of conclusion does this design support?
choices: It supports generalising from the sample to the population, but not a causal claim.
It supports a causal conclusion about the treatment, within the population studied.
It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.

items.prompt: A random sample of 2500 people gives a sample proportion of 47%. Using the conservative margin of error 1/√n, give the approximate margin of error and the resulting interval.
choices: ±0%, giving 47% to 47%
±2%, giving 45% to 49%
±4%, giving 43% to 51%
±47%, giving 0% to 94%

items.prompt: In 500 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 10 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 2% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 2% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
The simulation proves that there is no difference.

choices: It supports both generalisation and causation, provided the sample is large.
It supports neither generalisation nor causation, because self-selection can bias both.

choices: ±75%, giving 0% to 150%
±8%, giving 67% to 83%
±4%, giving 71% to 79%

items.prompt: In 100 simulations under the assumption of no difference, 2 produced a result at least as extreme as the one observed. What should be concluded?
choices: The observed result is not statistically significant: it occurred in 2% of simulations, which is not unusual.
The observed result is statistically significant: it occurred in only 2% of simulations, below the usual 5% threshold.
The simulation proves that the observed difference is real.
